Design Patterns Map Reduce

Disadvantage of map reduce: difficult to structure like map and reduce functions

Design patterns:

  1. In-mapper Combining
  1. Pairs and stripes
  1. Patterns for relational algebra operators
  1. Patterns for matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication

In-Mapper Combining

Intermediate data are:

  1. written locally
  1. transferred from mappers to reducers over network

Issues: bottleneck (network and disk writing)

Solution: reducing intermediate data

  1. combiners → it has some problems, so we can choose another combiner
    • Hadoop does not guarantee the execution of a combiner
  1. In-Mapper Combining

Stateless In-Mapper Combining

Intermediate form to understand the final solution

  • aggregate line by line
  • stateless since among invocations of the function we do not save the associative array

Stateful In-Mapper Combining

Initialize method → is the setup method (only once before map invocations)

Close method → is the

  • associative array is shared among all invocations of map function

  • Advantages:
    1. Combinersare provided as an optimization to the execution framework, which has the option of using it or not at all (maybe if resource constrained environment will not be executed)
    1. Combiners only reduce the amount of intermediate data that is transferred across the network but do not reduce intermediate data emitted by mappers in the first place and stored on local disk.
    • in mapper combiner provides complete control on the local aggregation and remove the overhead to disk writing
  • Disadvantages:
    • Memory management is more complex. No automatic spilling is performed as it happens with an external combiner. Therefore, the internal associative array may no longer fit in memory. Solved by:
      1. Either emitting intermediate data after processing every n input records rather than all of them
      1. Or monitoring memory footprint and emit intermediate data once memory usage has exceeded a certain threshold
      • How big the threshold or the number n? tradeoff between efficency of combininers and memory usage

Matrix Generation

Vector of size NNN﻿ → output will generate a matrix N×NN \times NN×N﻿

Example: word co-occurrence matrix

  • Given a document collection (vector of words of len NNN﻿), emit the bigram counts
  • Where NNN﻿ is the number of unique words
  • Cell mijm_{ij}mij​﻿ contains the number of times word wiw_iwi​﻿ co-occurs with word wjw_jwj​﻿
  • Used for example in statistical natural language processing

two solutions:

  1. pairs
  1. stripes

Pairs

  • only allocating space for the variable s, nothing else

Stripes

Relational Algebra Operators

Use case: seach engines

  • selection, projection, set operations (union, …), joins, grouping and aggregations

Selection

  • Map: each tuple ttt﻿ in RRR﻿, if condition c(t)c(t)c(t)﻿ is satisfied, is outputted as a (t,⊥)(t, ⊥)(t,⊥)﻿ pair
  • Reduce: for each(t,⊥,⊥,⊥,...) (t, ⊥, ⊥, ⊥, ...)(t,⊥,⊥,⊥,...)﻿ pair in input, output (t,⊥)(t, ⊥)(t,⊥)﻿


Projection

  • Map: each tuple ttt﻿ in RRR﻿, create a new tuple t′t't′﻿ containing only the projected attributes and output a (t′,⊥)(t', ⊥)(t′,⊥)﻿ pair
  • Reduce: for each (t′,⊥,⊥,⊥,...)(t', ⊥, ⊥, ⊥, ...)(t′,⊥,⊥,⊥,...)﻿ pair in input, output (t′,⊥)(t', ⊥)(t′,⊥)﻿

Union (automatic on spark)

  • Map: for each tuple ttt﻿ in RRR﻿ and SSS﻿, output a (t,⊥)(t, ⊥) (t,⊥)﻿ pair
  • Reduce: for each input key ttt﻿, there will be 1 or 2 values equal to ⊥⊥⊥﻿. Coalesce them in a single output (t,⊥)(t, ⊥)(t,⊥)﻿

Intersection

  • Map: for each tuple ttt﻿ in RRR﻿ and SSS﻿, output a (t,⊥)t, ⊥)t,⊥)﻿ pair
  • Reduce: for each input key ttt﻿, there will be 1 or 2 values equal to ⊥⊥⊥﻿. If there are 2 value, coalesce them in a single output (t,⊥)(t, ⊥)(t,⊥)﻿, otherwise do nothing

Difference (what is in RRR﻿, which is not in SSS﻿)

  • Map: for each tuple ttt﻿ in RRR﻿, output (t,R)(t , R)(t,R)﻿ and for each tuple ttt﻿ in SSS﻿, output (t,S)(t , S)(t,S)﻿
  • Reduce: for each input key ttt﻿, there will be 1 or 2 values. If there is 1 value equal to (t,R)(t , R)(t,R)﻿ output (t,⊥)(t, ⊥)(t,⊥)﻿, otherwise do nothing

Natural Join: assume we have two relations R(A,B)R(A,B)R(A,B)﻿ and S(B,C)S(B,C)S(B,C)﻿. Find tuples that agree on the B attribute values and output them.

  • Map: for each tuple (a,b)(a, b)(a,b)﻿ from RRR﻿, output (b,(R,a))(b, (R, a))(b,(R,a))﻿ and for each tuple (b, c) from SSS﻿, produce (b,(S,c))(b, (S, c))(b,(S,c))﻿
  • Reduce: For each input key bbb﻿, there will be a list of values of the form (R,a)(R, a)(R,a)﻿ or (S,c)(S, c)(S,c)﻿. Construct all pairs and output them together with bbb﻿. Emit ((a,b,c),⊥)((a, b, c), ⊥)((a,b,c),⊥)﻿

Grouping and Aggregation For simplicity, assume we have the relation R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C)﻿ and we want to group-by AAA﻿ and aggregate on BBB﻿.

  1. discard attrubute CCC﻿
  1. group by AAA﻿ (put all together)
  1. aggregate (like sum, avg, …) by BBB﻿

  • Map: for each tuple (a,b,c)(a, b, c)(a,b,c)﻿ from RRR﻿, output (a,b)(a, b)(a,b)﻿. Each key a represents a group.
  • Reduce: apply the aggregation operator to the list of bbb﻿ values associated with group keyed by aaa﻿, producing xxx﻿. Then output (a,x)(a, x)(a,x)﻿.

Matrix Multiplication

The matrix does not fit in memory (huge m), and

  1. The vector v does fit in a machine's memory (small n)
  1. The vector v does not fit in machine's memory (huge n)

Vector fit in memory

The matrix is stored in HDFS as a list of (i,j,mij)(i, j, m_{ij})(i,j,mij​)﻿ tuples

  • The elements vjv_jvj​﻿ of vvv﻿ are available to all mappers
  • Map: ((i,j),mij)(( i, j ), m_{ij})((i,j),mij​)﻿ pair → (i,mijvj)(i, m_{ij}v_j)(i,mij​vj​)﻿ pair
  • Reduce: (i,[mi1v1,...,minvn])(i, [m_{i1}v_1, ..., m_{in}v_n])(i,[mi1​v1​,...,min​vn​])﻿ pair → (i,mi1v1+...+minvn)(i, m_{i1}v_1 + ... + m_{in}v_n)(i,mi1​v1​+...+min​vn​)﻿ pair

Vector doesn’t fit in memory

  • Divide the vector in equal-sized sub-vectors that can fit in memory
    • divide them in files (eg. blue, green, …)
  • According to that, divide the matrix in stripes
  • Use the previous algorithm for each stripe/subvector pair

Matrix-Matrix multiplication

A matrix can be seen as a 4-attributes relation

  • (Matrix name, row index, column index, value) tuples
    • M → (M,i,j,mij)(M, i, j, m_{ij})(M,i,j,mij​)﻿, N → (N,j,k,njk)(N, j, k, n_{jk})(N,j,k,njk​)﻿
  • As large matrices are often sparse (0's) we omit such tuples
